title: My Pill Tastes Sweet Today
youtube_title: Five months pregnant, she bit her pill. Why was it sweet?
logline: Five months pregnant, Nora Quinn only wants to carry her baby safely to term. But the pill her husband left out this morning tastes sweet, and by night the phone by her bed is gone.
hook: A silent dream: the Glass House on the bluff breaks apart pane by pane from the roof down, shards hanging in midair; a crooked glass bird falls, and a hand reaches into frame and catches it. She wakes to a glass of warm water and one pill. She bites down and frowns: “My pill tastes sweet today.”
mid_hook: Afternoon. The doorbell. Cole, Grant's driver, stands there in white gloves: “Mr. Whitlock sent me.” “Your phone's going in for repair.” She hands it over. The door shuts, and the whole glass house goes quiet except for the waves.
extra_hooks: Peg stands in the nursery doorway, staring at the floor-to-ceiling window: “Window that big.” “The whole street can see in.” She picks the half-knitted hat up off the couch: “Stitches are loose.” “It'll come out too big.”
conflict: She wants to do what Dr. Brandt told her: rest, take her pills, get through the days. But the pill tastes wrong. She calls Grant and he laughs it off, “They changed the coating, babe,” then says her phone keeps dropping calls and he'll send his driver to take it in for repair. Peg makes her weekly visit to find fault: the soup's bland, the nursery window's too big.
turn: After a whole day of nitpicking, Peg leaves, and there's a pot of soup in the fridge with a note on the lid: “Salt's on you.” On TV, an ad: Grant cradling the Forever vase she blew at twenty-five, bowing slightly; the label reads only “Whitlock Home.” She looks at the half pill again. One letter of the imprint is fainter than usual.

cliffhanger.text: Past midnight, a cramp jolts her awake. She reaches for the nightstand. Empty. The phone never came back. She edges along the cold glass wall, and every pane reflects only her, alone.
cliffhanger.question: No phone. Who does she call?

spectacle: In the dream the Glass House splits pane by pane from the roof down, the shards hanging in the air without falling; a crooked glass bird drops through them and a hand catches it cleanly.
glamour_shot: Morning light through the floor-to-ceiling glass: Nora in a cream knit sweater, long hair loose, holds the half pill up to the window and squints at the imprint, her profile as still as glass.
general_payoffs: She wraps the spat-out half pill in a tissue and tucks it in her coat pocket instead of throwing it away
Peg calls the soup bland, then leaves a pot of it in the fridge
locations: The Glass House (bedroom, dining table, nursery)
The Glass House front door

title: The Light at the End of the Hall
youtube_title: No phone, no husband. Then a stranger stopped and made the call
logline: She drags herself to the front door for help, and a stranger whose face she never sees calls an ambulance. In the seventh-floor hallway at Merrow General, the one who comes isn't her husband. It's a doctor saying “I'm so sorry.”
hook: She pulls on her coat, the half-knitted hat still in her fist, and inches along the glass wall to the front door. Rain hits her face. She grabs the lamppost by the door; its light flickers.
mid_hook: A car brakes hard on the drive, headlights cutting through the rain. We see only a left hand dialing 911, an old burn scar across the back: “Glass House, on the bluff.” “Pregnant woman.” “Hurry.”
extra_hooks: Merrow General, the seventh-floor hallway with no windows. At the far end a light flickers. On the bench beneath it, a soaked figure sits down, face in shadow.
conflict: She has to hold on until someone comes. But her phone is gone, she's alone in the house, and her husband can't be reached all night.
turn: The one who saves her isn't her husband. It's someone whose face she can't make out. In the ambulance a voice keeps saying in her ear, “Stay awake.” The voice is all she remembers.

cliffhanger.text: Dr. Brandt crouches by her bed and pauses a beat: “I'm so sorry.” Nora is still clutching the hat. Nurse Kim gently slips it into a paper bag. At the end of the hall, the light flickers again.
cliffhanger.question: Where was her husband?

spectacle: A rainy night on the drive: the lamppost at the Glass House door flickering, headlights breaking through the rain to stop at her feet; Merrow General's seventh floor, a long windowless hallway, the light at its end going bright, dark, bright.
glamour_shot: Rain runs down her long hair as she holds the lamppost and looks up; the headlights wash her pale profile cold blue.
general_payoffs: A stranger calls the ambulance for her
The hat stays in her hand the whole way and ends up in the hospital's paper bag

title: We're Still Young
youtube_title: She waited alone till dawn. He said: “We're still young.”
logline: Nora needs to know where her husband was that night. He arrives at dawn and says he was at his mom's and his phone died. But his phone keeps lighting up.
hook: Dawn. The elevator opens. Grant's umbrella is still dripping, his rimless glasses fogged. He takes her hand, his voice warm as a keynote: “We're still young.”
mid_hook: Nurse Kim changes the IV and says softly: “The man who called 911?” “Not your husband.” “Some man.” “He didn't leave a name.” Nora turns to Grant. He's looking down, wiping his glasses.
extra_hooks: He says: “I was at Mom's.” “My phone died.” The words are barely out when the phone in his jacket buzzes. Then again.
conflict: She needs to know where her husband was and why she couldn't reach him. All he gives her is “I was at Mom's” and “My phone died.”
turn: She thought he was just late. One line from the nurse, “Not your husband,” and a phone that's supposedly dead but won't stop buzzing: for the first time, she knows he's lying.

cliffhanger.text: He steps out to the nurses' station. On the nightstand his phone lights up: “Got the curtain measurements. —S.” She stares at that S. He comes back and, without a word, flips the phone face down.
cliffhanger.question: Who is S.? Why the curtains?

spectacle: The seventh-floor hallway at dawn, the light at the end still flickering; a dripping black umbrella propped by the door, a small puddle on the floor reflecting the flicker.
glamour_shot: Dawn light slices through the blinds onto her pale profile and the long hair spread on the pillow. She watches that phone, and for the first time her eyes go cold.
general_payoffs: She learns his dead phone was a lie
She learns the ambulance was called by a man who left no name
locations: Merrow General, seventh-floor room
Merrow General, seventh-floor hallway

title: The Old One Couldn't Be Fixed
youtube_title: He brought her a new phone. Not one number in it. Not even her doctor's
logline: Nora wants to tell Grant about the sweet pill, but he hands her a new phone first, and every line she had to the outside world is gone.
hook: He pockets the face-down phone and pulls a new box from a paper bag: “The old one couldn't be fixed.” “Got you a new one.” She turns it on. The contacts list is empty.
mid_hook: She says: “That pill.” “It was sweet.” He smiles and tucks the blanket around her: “You're exhausted.” “The doctor said you'd overthink things.”
conflict: She wants her husband to hear “The pill was sweet.” With one “You're exhausted” he takes the words away, and he swaps out her phone, her number, and every person she could call for help.
turn: She thinks the new phone is thoughtful. Then she finds her old number disconnected; Dr. Brandt, her friends, her old studio, all gone. Her only line to the world now runs through him.

cliffhanger.text: He gets up, lifts her coat off the chair, and slides a hand into the pocket: “I'll take this home and wash it.” “Bring you a clean one tomorrow.” His fingers stop on the wad of tissue.
cliffhanger.question: Will he find the half pill?

spectacle: A brand-new phone glows on the white sheet; the contacts list scrolls down, row after empty row.
glamour_shot: Propped up in the hospital bed, she writes Dr. Brandt's office extension on her palm in ballpoint, lashes lowered, the fine glassblowing burns on the inside of her wrist faint in the morning light.
general_payoffs: She memorizes Dr. Brandt's office extension and writes it on her palm
locations: Merrow General, seventh-floor room

title: The Wall at the End of the Hall
youtube_title: Her mother-in-law came packed for a month. Then she went quiet
logline: Nora has to keep the half pill in her pocket. Her mother-in-law arrives with a suitcase, sharp-tongued as ever, then stands a long time at the wall at the end of the hall.
hook: She clamps a hand over the coat: “I'm cold.” Grant pauses, then smiles and lets go, draping the coat back over her shoulders: “Okay.” “No washing.” Her hand slides into the pocket and closes tight around the tissue.
mid_hook: Peg steps off the elevator with a big suitcase and a thermos of soup. She walks right past the room, down to the flickering light at the end of the hall. She looks at the blank wall and touches it once.
extra_hooks: Peg comes in and plants the thermos on the table: “Drink.” “It's bland.” “You like bland, right?” The suitcase holding a month of clothes stands beside the bed.
conflict: Before discharge she has to protect the half pill in her pocket and deal with her mother-in-law. Grant books her a car home and drives off ahead with his mother and the luggage.
turn: She thought Peg came to gloat. Instead Peg packed a month of clothes to move into the Glass House and cook for her. And in her son's car, something drains the color from Peg's face.

cliffhanger.text: In Grant's car, Peg opens the glovebox for a tissue and her fingers touch a folded receipt. One glance and she freezes. Her son watches her in the rearview mirror: “Mom?” “What's wrong?” She folds it small and tucks it into her ledger: “Nothing.”
cliffhanger.question: What did Peg find in the car?

spectacle: At the end of the windowless seventh-floor hallway, an old woman in a worn cardigan stands under the flickering light, palm flat against a blank wall; each time the light blinks, her shadow breaks.
glamour_shot: Nora sits on the edge of the bed, coat pulled around her shoulders, watching Peg's back through the doorway, long hair over her cream sweater, her wariness slowly turning to confusion.
general_payoffs: The half pill is safe, still in her coat pocket
Peg arrives with a month of luggage to move into the Glass House and cook
locations: Merrow General, seventh-floor room
Merrow General, end of the seventh-floor hallway

title: They Changed the Locks
youtube_title: Home from the hospital, her key won't turn. His lawyer has papers
logline: Home from the hospital, Nora's key won't turn. Her husband's lawyer is waiting inside with a property agreement she never signed, and it carries her signature.
hook: The car stops at the top of the drive. She climbs out holding the hospital bag and puts her key in the Glass House lock. It won't turn. She tries again. The lock is new, so shiny it hurts.
mid_hook: The door opens from inside. A man with slicked-back hair and gold-rimmed glasses, fountain pen in hand: “Mrs. Whitlock.” “Leonard Fisk, Grant's attorney.” “Two documents.” “One for you to sign.” “One you already signed.”
extra_hooks: In the living room, installers are hanging heavy grey curtains over the floor-to-ceiling glass. A woman with short hair and red lipstick directs them in heels: “Left side, a little more.” “This house is too see-through.”
conflict: She wants into her own home. Leonard Fisk blocks the door: divorce papers waiting for her signature, and a separate property agreement saying she already gave Grant everything.
turn: She thought the lock was broken. The whole house is no longer hers: the house, the accounts, even the design rights to the Forever vase she blew, all on a page with her signature. And the woman hanging curtains is the S. from the text: Sienna Vale, brand director at Whitlock Home.

cliffhanger.text: The last page of the property agreement: her name on the signature line, in her handwriting. Fisk adjusts his glasses: “The house, the accounts.” “The Forever design rights.” “You gave Grant all of it.” She stares at the signature: “I never signed that.”
cliffhanger.question: Then who signed it?

spectacle: In the house made of glass, installers hang heavy grey curtains panel by panel; the sea view disappears piece by piece and the room keeps getting darker.
glamour_shot: She stands in the middle of the darkening living room, hospital bag held to her chest, the last strip of sea light on her face as if that's about to be taken too.
general_payoffs: She says it up front, “Door's open.” “I'm coming in.”, and Fisk can't keep her out
She learns who S. is: Sienna Vale, Whitlock Home's brand director, there to hang curtains
locations: The Glass House (front door, living room)

title: Ten Minutes
youtube_title: Ten minutes to pack. She left the jewelry and took her mom's glass
logline: Nora has ten minutes to take what's hers. No jewelry, no money. Only her sketches from before the marriage and her mother's glass piece, the Keepsake block.
hook: Fisk taps the signature line: “It's in writing.” She says: “I want to see him.” Sienna signs the curtain delivery slip left-handed, without looking up: “Grant's busy.”
mid_hook: At the nursery door, an installer lifts a curtain rod: “This one too?” Sienna: “That one too.” Nora stops in the doorway and doesn't go in. The big window disappears inch by inch behind grey fabric.
extra_hooks: A suitcase stands by the front door, zipper half open, her clothes folded by someone else's hands. Fisk checks his watch: “Ten minutes.” “Personal items only.”
conflict: Fisk gives her ten minutes for personal items. Everything in the house has been listed as community property; in ten minutes she has to decide what truly belongs to her.
turn: Fisk says everything is community property, but the block on the shelf isn't anywhere on his list. Grant never thought it was worth anything. She picks up the Keepsake block, then pulls a thin folder from the bottom shelf in the study: “Sketches from before the wedding.” “Mine.”

cliffhanger.text: She carries the glass block to the door. Fisk holds out the divorce papers and the pen again: “Sign.” “Easier for everyone.” Her hand hovers above the pen.
cliffhanger.question: Does she sign the divorce?

spectacle: Grey fabric swallows the nursery window inch by inch until the last strip of sea light slips out through the gap, leaving only the ceiling light.
glamour_shot: Nora lifts the Keepsake block in both hands; afternoon light passes through it and lays a pale green glow on her fingertips and chin.
general_payoffs: She takes her mother's Keepsake block; it isn't on the property list
She takes a folder of signed sketches from before the marriage
locations: The Glass House (living room, nursery doorway, study, front door)

title: I'm Going with Her
youtube_title: She walked down the hill alone. Then her mother-in-law followed
logline: Nora won't sign and rolls her suitcase down the drive. Grant waits in his car for her to give in, and the first one out of that car is his mother.
hook: She pulls her hand back: “I never signed that one.” “I don't accept it.” “And this one?” “I won't sign.” She takes her suitcase, holds the glass block, and walks past Fisk.
mid_hook: Grant's car waits at the bottom of the drive, engine running. The window slides halfway down, phone still in his hand: “Nor, stop this.” “Sign it.” “I'll write you a check.” She doesn't break stride.
extra_hooks: In the passenger seat, Peg holds her ledger and looks through the windshield at the Glass House up the hill as its curtains close one by one.
conflict: Grant waits in the car for her signature and offers money. All she has is a suitcase and a block of glass: no money, no phone numbers, nowhere to go.
turn: We expect her to be pushed back up the hill to sign. She doesn't even look at the car. And no one expects the mother-in-law in the passenger seat to open her door, haul her own month's suitcase out of the trunk, and go after her down the hill.

cliffhanger.text: Peg drags her suitcase down the drive and stops beside Nora, out of breath, without a glance at her son: “I'm going with her.” Behind them, Grant bursts out of the car: “Mom!”
cliffhanger.question: Why is Peg going with her?

glamour_shot: She rolls her suitcase down the hill, sea wind tangling her long hair, the glass block in her arms catching the sunset, her back very straight.
general_payoffs: She doesn't sign the divorce papers
Peg gets out of her son's car and stands with her

title: Make Your Own Dinner, Grant
youtube_title: His mom left with the wife he threw out: “Make your own dinner”
logline: Nora looks for somewhere to spend the night with the mother-in-law who followed her. Peg complains about everything and explains nothing.
hook: Peg doesn't look back: “Make your own dinner, Grant.” Grant stands in the middle of the drive, phone still at his ear, and for the first time doesn't know what to say next.
mid_hook: At the Harborview Motor Inn's front desk, Bev unwraps a peppermint and sizes them up: “Two women.” “Two suitcases.” “Bad fight?” Peg: “In-laws.” The peppermint drops from Bev's fingers: “In-laws? Running off together?”
conflict: Night is coming: two women, two suitcases, and Nora doesn't have one card she's sure still works. Peg came with her, but Nora can't tell whose side Peg is really on.
turn: She thought Peg was just spiting her son. The moment they're in the room, Peg writes the room down in her ledger and moves both beds' blankets to Nora's side. But the paper Peg hides in the ledger cover behind her back makes Nora wonder, for the first time, what Peg knows.

cliffhanger.text: In the bathroom mirror she sees Peg, back turned, slip a small folded paper into the lining of the ledger cover, press it flat, then press it flat again.
cliffhanger.question: What's in Peg's ledger?

spectacle: Dusk at a bus stop: an old woman and a young one, two suitcases side by side; across the harbor the cranes light up in a row of red.
glamour_shot: Under the motel's yellow lamp she sits on the edge of the bed with her hair down, holding the glass block; the red neon outside blinks on and off across her face.
general_payoffs: Peg pays for the room; they have a place for the night
Grant is left standing on the drive and goes back to the Glass House alone

title: Half a Pill
youtube_title: Her first night thrown out, she tasted the half pill. Peg looked away
logline: Her first night out of the house, Nora takes out the half pill she's hidden all day. Peg takes one look and turns away, tells her they'll see the doctor tomorrow, and won't say what she knows.
hook: Nora comes out of the bathroom. Peg has already closed the ledger tight and is writing the last line: “Room, eighty-nine.” She sets down the pen, takes the half-knitted hat from the hospital bag, and looks at the loose stitches: “Stitches are loose.” Not another word. She tucks it into her own knitting bag.
mid_hook: Nora takes the tissue from her coat pocket and unfolds it layer by layer: the bitten half pill, imprint up. She touches it with the tip of her tongue. Sweet.
extra_hooks: Through the gap in the curtains: a black car across the street, lights off, a figure in the driver's seat, not moving.
conflict: All she has is half a sweet pill, and nobody believes her. The one person who might know the truth, Peg, keeps her mouth shut tighter than her ledger.
turn: She expects Peg to tell her not to overthink it. Instead Peg says, “We see the doctor tomorrow.” A woman who has taken her son's side all her life is, for the first time, telling Nora to look into him.

cliffhanger.text: Peg stares at the half pill a long time, then turns her face away: “We see the doctor tomorrow.” Nora asks: “Peg, what do you know?” Peg reaches over and switches off the lamp: “Go to sleep.” In the dark, the red neon outside blinks on and off across Peg's open eyes.
cliffhanger.question: What does Peg know?

spectacle: Under the lamp, an unfolded tissue holds the bitten half pill, imprint up, smaller than a lens of the reading glasses beside it.
glamour_shot: She sits on the edge of the bed holding the half pill up to the lamp, long hair over one shoulder, and for the first time her eyes say she will see this through.
general_payoffs: The half pill survives and becomes her first piece of evidence
Peg puts the half-knitted hat away in her own knitting bag
